content.thinking:
I'm planning a treasure hoard prop group in a stylized LoL aesthetic—exaggerated shapes, saturated glowing accents, readable from top-down. I'm figuring out whether I need joints at all, since most parts are static except lids, and checking whether a root joint is still required even without moving parts.

I'm settling on a root joint "base" plus a hinge joint "lidHinge" for the chest lid. The design centers on a coin mound (~0.8m radius, 0.5m tall), an ornate chest (~0.7×0.45×0.45m) with an open hinged lid, glowing gem clusters, a tall spiked crown, and a few tipped goblets, with extras like pearls or a ring for flavor. I'm picking a saturated gold/orange/teal/purple/crimson palette with dark navy chest wood trimmed in gold to match the hextech-inspired look.

For the overall footprint I'm targeting roughly 1.8×1.5m with a height near 1.1m counting the crown perched atop the mound. To stay within a 1000-part budget I'm merging hundreds of individual coins by color into a handful of combined geometries, using low-poly cylinders (~7-8 sides, 0.05m radius) scattered and tilted across an analytic dome heightfield to build the mound shape, with separate gold tone variants for visual variety.

I'm thinking through how to texture the coin faces -- designing simple gold and silver coin textures with a ring and rune/star emblem so the cylinder caps show a proper coin face, while accepting the side bands will just show a stretched sliver of the texture around the rim.

Simpler plan: keep the coin's cylinder body untextured in flat gold/silver, and only add a separate textured disc merged on top of the visible face for the coin artwork. This keeps merged-geometry attributes consistent across all the circle discs and cylinders, so the texture mapping via UVs still works correctly.

For the overall scene, I'm now laying out the heap: coins should have random tilts, mostly lying flat against the surface normal with some jitter for naturalness, plus a few standing stacks and a fan of spilled coins toward the front. I'm sketching the top-down layout — chest positioned back-center-left with an open lid hinged at the back, curved barrel-shaped lid built via an extruded profile.

For the lid specifically, I'm working out the extrude orientation so the arch shape reads correctly, and considering adding a thin velvet-lined inner layer so the inside is visible when opened at roughly 110°, possibly structuring it with a hinge joint so the lid parts sit in local coordinates.

Now I'm working out the hinge rotation math: the hinge sits along the X axis at the back edge, and I need the lid to swing from closed (extending forward) to open (swinging up and back), so I'm applying the standard rotation-about-X formulas to track how a forward-pointing point transforms as the angle increases.

With θ around -115°, the forward point lifts up and back correctly, confirming the sign convention. I'm defining the lid as a joint at the hinge position with a direction, so I can pose it after building the closed geometry, and I'm making sure all the lid's child parts are attached to that joint so they rotate together.

Now I'm designing the chest's visual details: indigo wood planks with gold corner brackets, straps, a glowing cyan gem lock plate, rivets, trim, and feet in an exaggerated LoL style, plus spiky corner flares and a hextech-style glowing lock, with a red velvet-lined interior filled with coins.

I'm building the chest as four walls plus a floor so the inside stays open, then placing a mounded gold coin heap that peeks above the rim and spills forward from the chest's front, partially burying its base while planning the heap's position, radius, and height so the chest still reads clearly behind the spilling treasure.

I'm plotting the heap's shape using layered bump functions across the ground plane — a main central mound plus smaller left and right ones, and a separate bulge inside the chest reaching near the rim — then considering building this as a custom heightfield mesh grid so coins can later be scattered across its surface.

For the base beneath the coins, I want the mesh to taper smoothly to zero height at the edges rather than leaving a flat gold square showing, so I'll drop any triangles where all vertices sit near the floor level, keeping the underlayer a darker gold tone slightly recessed below the coin positions.

Actually, I think a hexagonal stone dais would ground the whole scene better and read well from a top-down angle — something like a six-sided lathed base with glowing rune inlays and gold trim, roughly radius 1.15, with its top surface raised to about y=0.08 so everything else stacks above that baseline.

For the dais top I'm picturing a subtle emissive rune-ring decal, mostly hidden under the central heap but peeking out around the edges. Then I need to position a chest slightly off-center with a bit of rotational yaw for visual interest, building its geometry in local coordinates before transforming it into place.

Thinking through it more, applying yaw to the chest complicates things since extrudes and sweeps rely on directional vectors that would need rotating too, so I'll skip the yaw and keep the chest unrotated, relying on staggered placement of other elements for visual liveliness instead.

Now I'm sketching the chest's actual dimensions: a width and depth centered at a given position, with short feet, a body with thin walls, a floor box, and a thin crimson liner just inside the walls to suggest velvet interior, all merged together.

For the finish, I'm planning a wood grain paint mixing light and dark tones for the boxes, plus gold vertical straps on the front and full horizontal rim bands top and bottom, with L-shaped corner brackets topped by spiked gold crests for a dynamic, ornamented look.

For the lock, I'm shaping the plate as an extruded shield with a pointed bottom and a glowing cyan gem, with sphere rivets along the straps. For the lid, I'm working out how to build a curved barrel shape with a semi-elliptical profile, considering lofted extrusion versus a lathe-based approach, since the underside needs to read as a flat plane when the lid swings open.

When closed the half-ellipse's flat bottom faces down, but opening it 115° reveals that flat face toward the viewer, so I'm adding a thin crimson velvet slab there while the curved exterior stays visible from behind. For the gold bands across the lid, I'm building an arched ring profile by tracing the outer arc then the inner arc in reverse to form a strip, extruding it slightly proud of the surface, and reusing that helper for all three bands. I'm also positioning the hinge point in model space near the back edge before posing the whole lid.

Now I'm defining the lid profile coordinates relative to the hinge and setting up the extrusion axes so the shape is centered correctly, then moving on to designing a coin mound inside the chest as a localized height bump within the same heightfield function used for the rest of the terrain.

I'm working out the absolute height function for the chest dome so it peaks above the rim at the center and falls toward the walls, while making sure the outer coin heap only samples positions outside the chest footprint so nothing clips through the walls.

uct two heightfields instead: an outer heap excluded within the chest footprint, and an inner dome mesh confined to the chest interior, both sampled with coins. I'm estimating coin counts (roughly 380 outer, 120 inner, plus dais scatter) and working out triangle budgets per coin using low-segment cylinders for caps and sides.

I'm trimming the coin segment count and total count to fit the 60k triangle budget, settling on 8-sided cylinders with about 450 coins total for roughly 18k triangles, and checking the edge length against the fine-mesh threshold to confirm coins are small enough to qualify. Now I'm thinking through how to merge coins by colour variant—grouping gold, bright gold, amber, and silver coins, with a shared textured face decal applied per variant while the cylinder body colour varies underneath.

I'm settling on three face textures (gold, bright, silver) each with rune emblem variation, giving six mergeable parts total (body + face disc per kind), and working out how to orient the face disc on top of each coin using a quaternion built from the up vector plus jitter and spin, then composing the final transform matrix to clone and place each coin instance.

For merging, I need the cylinder and circle geometries to share the same attribute set (position, normal, uv, indexed) so they combine cleanly, with only the circles getting the face texture while the cylinder sides and bottom stay flat-colored. I'm offsetting the face disc slightly above the cap to avoid z-fighting, settling on about 1.5mm clearance, and skipping the extra rim paint ring for now. Next I'm moving on to designing the gem shapes — thinking through a faceted "brilliant cut" gem built from a lathe profile for a saturated, glowing look.

For the gems, I'm defining a lathe profile with table, crown, girdle, and pavilion points, using low segment counts so the shading reads as flat-faceted facets rather than smooth. I'm assigning rich colors per gem type and realizing that making all gems emissive/glowing would wash out the faceted shading into flat silhouettes, so I decide to keep most gems unlit with flat shading to preserve facet readability, reserving true glow effects only for hero crystals, runes, and small core spheres.

Trying a lower glow strength around 0.5-0.6 to see if it preserves some facet definition while still emitting light, planning to check this in a preview render.

For the crystals themselves, I'm thinking hextech-style hexagonal prisms with pointed tips, clustered in groups of 3-5 at the back corners of the dais in cyan and purple, glowing strongly as lathed six-sided shapes.

Writing texture gradient code...

For the cone tip, I realize reusing the same gradient texture would create a seam since the cone's v-mapping runs opposite to the prism's, so I need a separate reversed-gradient texture for the tip — meaning 4 textures total across cyan and violet (prism + tip each). For the gem heap, I'm thinking of mixing normal faceted lit gems with just a few glowing ones for variety.

Now I'm designing the crown as the centerpiece atop the heap, with an exaggerated LoL-style look: tall alternating spikes, a glowing central ruby, and a decorated band. I'm building the band as a hollow lathed frustum shell, then placing 8 spikes around it alternating tall and short, each extruded as a flame-like curved profile.

Each spike gets a gem sphere at its tip, and I'm tilting the whole crown slightly backward by treating it as a part with its own position and rotation applied in world space, so I can build the geometry in local coordinates first and then transform it.

I'm planning a helper system that collects geometries by color into a map, transforming and pushing clones while making sure everything gets indexed consistently before merging, since extrude geometry comes out non-indexed while lathe, box, and sphere geometries are indexed.

To solve the mixed-indexing problem that breaks merging, I'll normalize everything by converting to non-indexed geometry with just position, normal, and uv attributes. I'm leaning toward flat shading by default for the low-poly facet look, reserving smooth normals for specific cases like spheres, and now I'm second-guessing whether to use the SDK's own primitive builders instead of raw three.js constructs.

I'll mix both approaches: SDK helpers like extrude, lathe, and sweep for hero parts with curved forms (crown arches, goblet bowls, handles), since lathe/extrude support paint coordinates useful for banded detailing, while using merged raw geometry for repeated simple bits. I also need to keep painted surface area moderate since texel density depends on total painted area across the shared atlas, so I'm deciding to default to a 1024 paint sheet and limit detailed painting to hero surfaces only.

For the goblets, I'm planning three distinct pieces -- a tall gold one with rubies, a jeweled silver chalice tipped over spilling coins, and a smaller horn -- all built via lathe profiles with a foot disc, stem knob, and flared bowl, using a closed loop profile so the inner wall shows hollowness from above. I'll use low segment counts for a faceted look, add painted height-based bands for engraved patterns, and stud gems around the rim and knob.

I need to tilt the spilling chalice using the lathe's axis option so it rests naturally on the coin heap with a trail of coins spilling from its mouth, checking the resting point against the heap's height field. For the standing goblets, I'm placing the ruby one near the right-front of the dais and the amethyst one at the left-front atop the coin pile, working out positions in a top-down x,z layout where +X corresponds to the viewer's right since the camera faces -Z.

Now I'm plotting the coin heap geometry within the hexagonal dais: the chest sits centered toward the back, crystal clusters are placed left and right within the interior radius, and I'm scattering several overlapping bumps of varying size and height across the front area to build a naturalistic mounded pile of coins and gems.

I'm positioning the crown tilted and partially sunk into one of the taller bumps so it reads as resting on the pile, and working out where to place standing goblets so their bases align with the heap's surface height at each location rather than floating above it.

For the goblets themselves, I'm sketching three: a tall gold one with a ruby on one side, a silver-blue one with a sapphire on the other, and a third tipped over near the front spilling coins and gems toward the viewer to add dynamism to the composition.

I also want a draped pearl necklace curving over the heap and chest front with gem pendants, a gold ring or two with set stones lying loose, and maybe a small stack of gold ingots near the chest to round out the pile's variety.

For coins, I'll add standing coin-stack columns of varying heights scattered toward the right side using the same coin geometry with offsets, including one toppled leaning stack, plus dozens of loose coins scattered across the dais floor with random yaw and a few balanced on edge for realism.

For the chest, I'm keeping the interior simple with maybe a gem-studded pendant on the lid, plus a lock plate with a glowing hextech gem. I'll also add a ring of glowing hex-rune inlay lines on the dais floor using a textured plane positioned just above the lathe top to avoid z-fighting.

Switching to a hexagonal CylinderGeometry for the dais instead of a lathe, I need to figure out the vertex orientation — corners sit at ±Z with flat edges at ±X — so I can align the SVG rune ring plane correctly after rotating it into the XZ plane.

Now I'm planning the dais as two hexagonal tiers—a lower tier at radius 1.22 and height 0.05, topped by a slightly smaller tier at radius 1.1 reaching height 0.08—with a dark navy-stone base color and a lighter accent tone for contrast.

I'm adding a thin gold trim ring along the tier edges plus small gold cone studs at each of the six corners, then designing a hex rune texture: concentric teal hexagon outlines with tick marks and glyph shapes, rendered at high resolution for crisp line detail.

Restricting the glow texture to the rim annulus between 0.82 and 1.02 meters so the empty center stays covered by the central heap, and letting an emissive plane handle the dais glow. For top-down readability I'm locking in a saturated palette: layered golds from highlight to bronze, a deep navy-purple wood tone for the chest, and strong accent colors to pop against the base.

Finalizing accent hues...

Deciding I only need a simple glow effect, no toon shading, and planning just two hinge joints: the root and the lid. Now I'm setting up the TypeScript structure, importing Three.js and the geometry merge utility to start building the scene.

Setting up imports and batching logic...

For flushing, I'll merge normalized geometries per batch and emit a part call with bone, flat shading, texture, and glow strength if applicable; I'll keep separate stashes for root and lid bones. I'm writing a normalization helper that strips geometry down to just position, normal, and uv attributes, converting indexed geometry to non-indexed first.

I'm checking that flat shading recomputes normals correctly while smooth preserves them, and confirming that applying matrix transforms also updates normals properly, and that painted fills work fine on merged geometries since UV islands are handled by the harness. Now I'm sketching a coin-placement function that takes a kind, position, normal, and spin, with coin kinds defined by body color and other properties.

Building the coin geometry...

For orienting each coin I'm composing a transform matrix from position, a quaternion combining the tilted normal with a spin rotation, and scale. For the coin pile, I'm sizing radii between 0.042–0.056 with thickness 0.01, and estimating that around 500-560 coins with radius 0.05 gives enough density to cover the mound area with overlap.

Each coin body uses roughly 8-sided geometry (sides plus caps plus face triangles), totaling around 40 triangles per coin, so 560 coins lands near 22k triangles -- combined with other scene elements that stays under a reasonable 40k budget. I consider reducing segment count but keep 8 sides so round coins still read visually.

For placement, I'm using rejection sampling across the heap's footprint: picking random x,z points, computing height from the heightfield, filtering for points above a minimum height, and enforcing minimum spacing between coins via a spatial hash. Each coin's orientation comes from the local surface normal (via gradient) with some random tilt jitter added for a natural scattered look.

I'm aiming for about 520-560 coins covering roughly 2.2 square meters, using Poisson-disc-style spacing of 0.035, sampling ~6000 candidate points and accepting the first batch that fits. Most coins tilt slightly up to 10° based on slope, with about 10% standing more steeply (up to 70°) for visual variety, plus small random vertical jitter to create natural layering.

For the mound's base mesh, I'm building a plane subdivided 40x40 over the heap's footprint, displacing vertices by the heightfield and trimming low-height triangles manually via custom position/index arrays, flat-shaded and tinted a dark mottled gold so it reads as shadow between coins. I'm lowering it slightly so coins visually rest on top rather than floating.

I'm also scattering about 30 gems across the same sampled points using a separate list, generating low-poly bipyramid shapes via a lathe profile for a cheap faceted gem look.

Defining chest dimensions...

Adding plank seam lines...

Still writing noise-stretching code...

I'm also planning gold chest straps as thin boxes positioned on the front, sized to wrap toward the top edge.

Now I'm adding back straps, top rim bands, and bottom bands to frame the armor with a consistent gold trim, plus a helper function for placing these boxes. I'm also designing corner pieces with vertical gold guards, small pyramid-cap flares on top, and rows of tiny rivet spheres for detail.

For the feet, I'm going simple with slanted boxy gold blocks rather than full ball-and-claw designs. For the lock, I'm extruding a pointed shield-shaped plate to sit on the front of the body across the body-lid seam, keeping it attached to the body rather than the lid for simplicity.

I'll add a small flat gold tab with a hole on the lid itself, hanging down to act as the hasp tongue when closed. The gem on the lock is a glowing cyan octagon lathe shape with a ring of six small gold cone prongs around it, and the lid's curved profile will be shaped as an arch with an ellipse cross-section rising from the hinge.

Shaping lid curve...

Still designing lid paint bands...

I'm adding gold end plates to the lid by extruding a slightly scaled-up arch outline at each end, sizing and positioning them to align with the lid body width and the chest wall.

For the lid underside, I'm placing a crimson velvet slab facing downward so it's visible when the lid opens, plus small gold stud spheres arranged in a grid and a glowing gem inset at the center for detail. I'll skip adding lid stay chains and just group all these lid elements together under the lid's pivot bone.

Now I'm calculating the hinge rotation — swinging the lid back about -112° around the hinge point, working out how the trigonometry moves the lid's top edge upward and slightly backward so its front edge ends up around y=1.0, roughly matching the chest's total height when fully open.

Rechecking the hexagon dimensions for the dais — using R=1.1 gives better proportions, with x extent ±0.95 and z extent ±1.1. I'm verifying the chest and lid fit inside these hexagonal boundaries, accounting for how the slanted edges narrow the available depth away from the center.

That gives a wider frame, which works better visually. I'll rotate the hexagon by 30° so vertices sit at ±X and flat edges face ±Z, keeping the symmetry clean for the SVG drawing.

I'm checking that the dais, chest, lid, and crystal clusters all stay within the hexagonal boundary at the chosen radius, then setting up the height function for the terrain bumps using a radial falloff formula.

Checking that the main heap bump at the chest's front reaches the right height to blend smoothly into the chest footprint, confirming the chest front elevation lines up with where the lock plate sits.

Now I'm shaping the inner dome of coins inside the chest, defining a bulging height function over the interior footprint with some lumpy noise, planning for scattered coins and gems on top, plus a few coins draped over the front rim onto the wall. I'm starting to build the base mesh grid for this inner dome.

Next I'm working on the crown geometry resting on the heap, setting up a local coordinate frame tilted so the crown leans backward against the chest wall, figuring out the rotation angle needed around the X-axis to get that lean.

Defining crown lathe profile...

For spikes and gems I'll build helper functions that transform local coordinates into world space using a quaternion, giving tangent and outward-leaning spike directions. Setting crown spike count to 7.

I'm varying spike heights: a tall ornate center front spike around 0.26, alternating smaller ones at 0.19/0.13, going for an elongated LoL-style curvy silhouette with edge glow. I'm also considering adding gem balls at tips, a small rim of triangles, and possibly crossing gold arches rising to a central orb for a stronger readable top-down silhouette, even though the crown leans.

Deciding against cluttering with both arches and too many spikes, I'll settle on 8 spikes with gem tips plus a central ruby band gem, and add a velvet crimson liner dome inside the band that's visible from above, paired with two crossing gold arches over it for that classic crown look.

Now I'm planning the goblet function with its lathe profile — foot, stem, bowl — along with gem bezels, beaded rims top and bottom, and painted filigree diamond patterns on the band.

Still defining the lathe profile...

Now I'm adding handles for the chalice via catmull-rom sweeps, and placing a ring of eight small gems around each goblet's bowl using analytic angle positions with orientation quaternions aligned from up to the outward normal.

For the tipped goblet I'm tilting its lathe axis so it rests on the heap, pointing toward the viewer and rising slightly, with coins spilling from its mouth along a parabolic arc toward the pile below, making sure its lowest point stays above the heap surface. Now I'm starting the crystal cluster function, defining base position, height, radius, and tilt parameters.

Building the hex prism geometry with a cone tip, matching their UV mapping so brightness gradients flow smoothly from a dark base through to a glowing white apex.

Adding overlay shading...

For colors, I'm picking cyan going from deep blue at the base to pale icy cyan at the top, violet from deep purple to light lavender, with a small accent of ruby/pink crystals for warmth—building 6 small texture swatches total from these 3 palettes.

Now I'm planning glowing details: runes on the hex floor, glowing gem-like crystals set into a chest lock, and a scatter of tiny sparkling star-shaped cards floating above the gem heap, using small four-point star textures on double-sided cards facing upward for that magical glint effect.

I'm also adding a draped gold necklace sweeping over the hoard using a catmull path, with alternating gold beads and white pearl spheres along the chain, plus a pendant gem at the end.

For rings, I'm using small tori lying on the heap with a gem mounted on top, placing two of them. I'm shelving scepters and daggers for now, but I'm working out how to construct stacked ingots as frustum shapes using scaled cylinder geometry to get that tapered box look.

I'm now checking placement of the ingot stacks and coin towers against the hexagonal dais boundary, making sure positions near the edges still fit within the allowed radius so nothing clips off the platform.

I'm checking each bump and crystal placement against the hexagon's narrowing boundary at different z-values, confirming the main bump and smaller clusters stay within limits, then verifying ingot and crystal positions near the edges fit too.

I need to shrink bumps B and C since they conflict with the ingots' position, then I'm placing coin towers on the left and checking goblet positions against the shrinking boundary at their heights.

Checking bump D's radius against the floor level confirms goblets should stand clear on a flat area, so I'll surround the base with a skirt of scattered coins and gems for a fuller silhouette. I'm also sketching a third tipped goblet near bump D and considering a crown resting atop bump A.

Now I realize the crown placed centered at the chest front overlaps and hides the lock plate, since the camera's 3/4 angle puts the crown directly in front of it. I'll offset the crown to x=+0.28, z=0.28, tilt it back-left and angle it toward camera-left so the lock stays visible within its narrow x-range.

Thinking about silhouette hierarchy: tall open lid at back, crown mid-height in front of it, small goblets up front, plus a scattering of spilled coins leaning against the chest's front rim for visual interest and subtle gold dust detail. Designing a coin emblem icon...

I'll add a rare fourth coin variant with a cyan gem center, and set distribution percentages: gold 45%, amber 25%, silver 15%, rare 15%. Then I'll move on to designing the dais with a mottled stone texture.

Now I'm starting the builder code, defining the root joint and the lid's hinge joint, working out the hinge direction and bone orientation carefully.

I'm sketching out a Stash helper class to accumulate fills, geometries, and options per joint before flushing them, and checking which types I need to import like Joint, Texture, and Paint for the fill parameter.

Writing matrix and geometry helpers...

Now I'm designing the heightfield mesh builder, computing vertex heights from the H function and skipping triangles that fall below the floor threshold, producing a non-indexed geometry for flat shading since painted parts likely get their own UV islands from the harness.

For coins resting beyond the mound heap, I'm setting up a separate scatter list with its own RNG seed, then moving on to define the color palette constants for gold, bronze, and wood tones used throughout the scene.

Still writing palette constants...

Finishing the gold gradient blend, then sketching stone paint with a mottled hex-plate pattern using cell-based tiling for the top surface.

For the stonework I'm defining irregular flagstone patches with crack lines splitting different stone shades, then setting up the heap base, velvet mottling, and the crown's filigree lattice paint function next.

Still writing lattice logic...

Now I'm moving on to the dais structure, building a hexagonal cylinder geometry with stone shading and defining tiered levels for the base.

Adding glowing orbs to the corner studs now, then designing a rune texture plane positioned just above the inner dais, working out the hexagonal path coordinates for the glowing rune ring in SVG.

Still have coins, crystals, ingots, necklace, and sparkles to design, needing sizes checked against the preview box. I'm double-checking the API signatures for lathe, extrude, sweep, and part functions before writing the coin emblems and sparkle star SVG.

I'm also figuring out card frame placement — orienting cards along the flow direction with a cross variant for side visibility, and positioning the root so the card center sits properly above the anchor point.

Now I'm working out the coin placement logic: computing surface normals from height field gradients, then scattering coins with slight height offset, randomized tilt angles (with a fraction standing upright), spin, and scale per coin.

I'm handling exclusions so coins don't spawn inside the chest, goblet bases, ingot stacks, or crown footprints, while still allowing hidden coins beneath objects. For density I'm using Poisson-disc sampling via grid hashing with a minimum distance, running up to 9000 attempts, plus a separate scatter pass for flat coins lying on the floor ring between the heap and dais.

For the gems, I'm running a separate random sampler constrained to higher terrain heights with its own minimum spacing, generating around 34 gems with varied size, tilt, and cycling type, positioned just above the surface. I'm also placing roughly 110 coins inside the chest's interior dome shape, oriented using the surface gradient, and now I'm working out how coins spill from the tipped goblet's mouth along its pour axis.

Still working out the arc trajectory for falling coins, blending horizontal drift with a parabolic drop clamped to the heap surface, placing about 9 coins mid-flight with randomized tilt to sell the pouring motion.

Now I'm designing a goblet-building function that takes position, axis, scale, and style parameters to generate a lathed shape with gold body, trim, and gem details. I'm considering whether to split the bowl into separate outer and inner-lining lathes so the interior wall can be painted a darker gold distinct from the outer surface.

I'm working out a normal-based paint rule: since the inner wall of the bowl faces upward/inward while the outer flare faces outward/downward, I can test the vertical component of the surface normal to decide which color to apply, though I need to restrict this by height so it doesn't accidentally darken the foot or knob surfaces too.

For a tilted goblet, the simple position-based test breaks down, so I'm considering a separate inner liner lathe object with its own fill color to simulate liquid or filled content -- maybe gems or jewels overflowing from the bowl for visual richness.

Simplifying: goblets will just have gems or coins piled visibly in the bowl rather than complex interior paint logic, with gold used everywhere except trim. One goblet gets decorative handle sweeps, and I'm working out the exact outline coordinates for the tall goblet's profile.

Still writing goblet outline coordinates...

Still checking wall thicknesses for crossing issues, confirming the inner and outer radii stay properly nested at each height before applying a uniform scale factor to set the goblet's overall height.

I'm scaling the tall goblet down to 0.29m to better match chest proportions, and sketching a separate silver chalice silhouette with a wider fluted bowl. I'm also planning a helper function to populate gem and coin positions within each bowl before writing the actual rendering code.

Setting up imports and type declarations...

Building a Stash class that groups geometries by a composite key based on fill, smoothing, texture, and glow settings, normalizing and transforming each geometry before merging them by group when flushed.

Writing matrix helper functions...

Now I'm working out coin geometry: a scaled unit cylinder for the body and a circle for the face, figuring out the right translation offset so the face sits just above the coin surface given the thin scale factor.

I'm also defining color palettes for coin kinds like gold, amber, and silver, plus setting up a weighted list of coin kinds and a helper function to place coins with position, normal, and spin. I'm extending this to gems too, mapping out a set of gem colors like ruby, sapphire, emerald, violet, topaz, and cyan.

For gem shapes I'm building a cached geometry function that generates a lathed "brilliant" cut from a profile of points, and I'm working through whether the lathe's face normals come out pointing outward correctly given the point ordering, checking the orientation for the culet, crown, and table faces.

I'll skip the emerald-cut shape for now and just use flat-fill materials per gem color, and plan to keep glow effects off for most gems except maybe a special "rare hero" one.

For the chest lock, I'm positioning a cyan-glowing brilliant-cut gem on the lock plate, lathing its profile along the forward axis and nudging it slightly proud of the plate surface so it reads clearly on the front face.

Now I'm working out the crown's placement and tilt, computing its origin to sit resting on the coin pile with a slight forward dip, and building a quaternion from yaw, pitch, and roll Euler angles in YXZ order to get the natural tilted-crown look.

So the crown leans back with the back rim sinking slightly into the coins for a natural resting look. For the spike shape, I'm defining a tall pointed outline that gets extruded and smoothed, scaled by height, and positioned around the band's top radius with a slight sink adjustment.

For orientation, I'm computing the tangent and outward normal at each spike's angle around the crown, flaring the extrusion direction slightly outward from vertical for a more natural splay. Each spike tip gets a small low-poly gem — cyan glow for tall spikes, ruby for short ones — and since each spike is its own extrude part, I can paint them gold individually without affecting the rest.

Now I'm also adding small inset gems at each spike's base, oriented so the gem's axis points along the outward normal with the culet facing inward, and sketching the two crossing arches as swept Catmull-Rom curves running from the front rim up over the crown and down to the back rim.

Shaping the orb and velvet cap...

Adding gems to the band at interpolated radius positions with outward-tilted normals, plus filigree paint on the lathe profile. Now varying the eight spike heights so the front spike is tallest as a hero element, alternating shorter heights around the crown for visual rhythm.

Writing chest box helpers...

Adding more box dimensions...

Adding cone caps atop the corner posts, checking lid clearance when open, then placing rivets, studs, and the four feet blocks beneath the chest.

Now I'm defining the lock plate as a shield-shaped extrusion mounted on the front, orienting its thickness along the z-axis so it faces outward correctly.

I'm adding the gem detail with a lathed shape at the lock center, plus a small dark keyhole box beneath it, and considering prong cones ringing the gem outward. For the hinges, I'm placing two gold cylindrical rods at the back-top edge, symmetric along x, to act as the barrel hinge for the lid.

Now I'm building out the lid itself: the arched body, several raised bands and end plates, a velvet-lined underside, decorative studs, and a tab-and-ring pull.
